groups.text: A service caches FX rate tables, each behind a WeakReference, so that the G C can free them if memory runs low.
Under normal load, the cache keeps missing.
After each G C, the tables are gone.
Memory wasn't low.
So why did the G C throw them away?
The G C frees what nothing can reach.
It starts from the roots: thread stacks, static fields, and references from native code.
It follows every reference, and keeps what it finds.
Everything else is garbage.
Ordinary references are strong.
The G C leaves their objects alone.
A SoftReference may be cleared when memory gets tight, and must be cleared before an OutOfMemoryError.
A WeakReference holds nothing up.
The next G C that finds the object clears it.
A PhantomReference never gives you the object: get() always returns null.
It only tells you the object is gone.
Some time after clearing a reference, the G C can put it on a ReferenceQueue.
The spec gives no deadline.
So the weak cache forgets at every G C, which on a busy service is milliseconds away.
A soft cache fails the other way.
A sixty-four MB heap holds a forty MB rate table behind a soft reference, and the code asks for forty MB more.
What does the G C do?
A full G C keeps the table, and still finds no room.
A second full G C clears the soft reference, and the allocation goes through.
Now every request reloads the table at once, while the heap is under pressure.
So give your cache a maximum size and an expiry time, and size the heap for it.
In Java and in Kotlin, a weak reference with its queue looks like this.
The rule: the G C keeps what the roots can reach.
Soft holds until memory is tight, weak until the next G C, and phantom not at all.
Quick check. A listener is held only through a WeakReference.
Does it survive the next G C?
No. Nothing strong holds it.
